y8-6: The study comes from a single region and is observational; it does not prove that substance use or any other factor caused the rise. Still, stroke is not only a problem of older age: if sudden symptoms such as a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech appear, call 112 straight away, whatever your age.
y8-7: In a study published in Neurology on 23 September 2026, which examined 2,076 strokes in adults aged 20 to 54 in the Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky region of the US between 1993 and 2020, the stroke rate in this age group rose from 33.9 to 62.2 per 100,000, an increase of about 83%. Stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel (ischaemic stroke) rose from 23.8 to 47.3 per 100,000. Among people who had a stroke, the share reporting substance use rose from 4.6% to 40.2%, largely driven by cannabis. Over the same period, the death rate within 30 days of a stroke fell from 11.7% to 9.4%.

y8-9: This is a cross-sectional study based on measurements taken at a single point in time, in volunteers in England; a single reading is not enough for a diagnosis. High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so having yours checked regularly matters. If you take medication, you can talk to your doctor about whether you are reaching your target.
y8-10: In a study published in BMJ Public Health, researchers at the University of Oxford examined blood pressure readings from about 1.4 million adults who joined the Our Future Health programme in England between 2022 and 2025. 37% of participants had high blood pressure: 15% of those aged 18–39 and 71% of those aged 80 and over. After adjusting for age, the figure was 42% in men and 29% in women. 59% of those with high blood pressure had never been diagnosed or treated, and half of those taking blood pressure medication still had readings of 140/90 or higher.

y8-13: This is an observational study: it does not prove that loneliness causes disease. The researchers plan clinical trials to test cause and effect. Even so, the finding suggests that the feeling of loneliness may not be offset by healthy habits alone, and that relationships deserve attention in their own right.
y8-14: In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers at Tulane University in the US followed 277,489 adults aged 40 to 69 who at the start had no diabetes, heart disease, lung disease, dementia, cancer, depression or anxiety. At age 50, people who both felt lonely and were socially isolated, compared with those who were neither, lost about 2.4 years (women) and 1.7 years (men) of life free of physical disease, and about 3.7 years (women) and 5.8 years (men) of life free of depression and anxiety. Habits such as a healthy diet, exercise, good sleep and not smoking reduced the loss linked to social isolation, but did not significantly reduce the loss linked to loneliness.
